title: Design Thinking: how to solve problems creatively and with people at the center
description: Design Thinking beyond sticky notes: a human-centered approach to solving problems, with pillars, examples and how to apply it day to day.

related.title: Servientrega
related.body: In practice: a complex journey turned into a simple visual experience.

blocks.text: What comes to mind when you hear “Design Thinking”? Maybe an intense brainstorming session with sticky notes all over the room? Despite that popular image, Design Thinking is much more than a collaboration technique. It's a powerful, human-centered approach to solving problems that puts people at the center of every decision.
Want to see how it can transform your design process? Come with me!

At the heart of Design Thinking is empathy: before creating any solution, the focus is on deeply understanding the needs, wants and experiences of the people who will be affected by the product or service.

Imagine you're designing a new app for college students. Instead of jumping into drawing interfaces, you take the time to talk to students and understand their routines, frustrations and what they really need to make life easier. This process doesn't just guide what you create, it also humanizes the solutions, making sure they make sense in the real world.

blocks.caption: Before drawing: listen, take notes and group them until the real problem shows up.

blocks.text: Imagine a chef who wants to create a new dish for the restaurant's menu. He could just test flavor combinations on his own, but instead he decides to talk to the customers. He asks about their preferences, tries out different recipes and gathers feedback before settling on the final dish.

blocks.caption: The chef's cycle from the article: listen, create and adjust with the people who will use it.

blocks.text: This cycle of listening, creating and adjusting is the essence of Design Thinking. It's an iterative process that looks for the ideal solution by putting people at the center of creation.

blocks.caption: Each round of testing and adjusting makes the solution better than the last. It's the cycle, not the first idea, that gets it right.

blocks.text: Being “human-centered” goes beyond creating beautiful or functional products. It's about solving problems in a way that makes sense for the people who really matter: the users.

blocks.caption: The article's four pillars, in sequence.

blocks.text: Here are the main pillars of Design Thinking:

items: Empathy: Before thinking about solutions, it's essential to listen to stories, observe behavior and dive into the user's world. That lets you identify real problems that may not be obvious at first glance.
Defining Needs: When you understand users deeply, you can map their pain points and needs more accurately.
Co-Creation: Design Thinking values active collaboration. Bringing users in to help create the ideas enriches the process and makes sure the final solution really serves them.

Prototyping and Iteration: Instead of spending months building something perfect, Design Thinking encourages quick prototypes. These prototypes are tested, refined and adjusted based on user feedback.

blocks.text: How to Apply Design Thinking in Your Day to Day

items: In Digital Product Design: Before creating wireframes in Figma, interview users to understand their pain points and expectations.
In Marketing: Build campaigns from direct feedback from your target audience.
In Resolving Internal Conflicts: Use empathy to listen to everyone involved and co-create solutions that work for all.

blocks.text: When we put people at the center, we create more than effective solutions: we create emotional connections. Well-thought-out products and services don't just solve problems, they also delight people and build loyalty.
By adopting Design Thinking, you stop simply “creating for the market” and start creating for people.
What about you? Have you used Design Thinking in your work, or do you want to start? Share your experience in the comments! Let's swap ideas and learn together.
